st.t: Employment effects: Task substitution permits stable jobs
st.an: The source accepts that automation’s employment effects are mediated by multiple task-level mechanisms rather than mechanically producing job loss. It materially extends the cluster by modelling expertise substitution: removing task-based qualification barriers can initially expand occupational employment while compressing incumbent wages, even as aggregate output rises. Its results are theoretical and conditional on specific task-bundling and factor-supply assumptions.
qs: In the expertise model, automation has a third effect: it renders redundant the expertise that was formerly required to perform now-automated tasks.
Employment initially rises in                                                   7 ^Loccupations as they become inexpert, owing to the elimination of expertise requirements.

st.t: Job exposure: Which tasks vanish changes outcomes
st.an: The source accepts that automation outcomes depend on which tasks change rather than exposure or task counts alone, and materially extends the cluster by modelling how the removal of expert versus supporting tasks changes the scarcity of expertise, qualified labour supply, wages and employment. Its computerisation-era evidence is presented as illustrative rather than definitive for AI.
qs: Nevertheless, our expertise framework suggests a complementary but distinct conceptual focus for analyzing the relationship between automation and the value of labor: it is not merely                                                   52 ^Lthe quantity of tasks performed by an occupation or demographic group that determines demand for its labor, but also the scarcity of the expertise required to perform those tasks.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Autor and Thompson reinforce the cluster’s task-reconfiguration and heterogeneous labour-effects account while materially extending it: automation’s effects depend not only on which tasks change, but also on the scarcity of the expertise those tasks embody. This helps explain why AI may complement experts while pressuring less-knowledgeable workers, though their evidence is illustrative, economy-wide and drawn from the pre-generative-AI computer era rather than legal workflows directly.
qs: Nevertheless, our expertise framework suggests a complementary but distinct conceptual focus for analyzing the relationship between automation and the value of labor: it is not merely                                                   52 ^Lthe quantity of tasks performed by an occupation or demographic group that determines demand for its labor, but also the scarcity of the expertise required to perform those tasks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the task-level view of automation and materially extends the cluster’s labour analysis with an expertise-and-indivisibility framework: employment and wage effects depend not only on how many tasks are automated, but on the expertise composition of the tasks retained. Its 1980–2018 occupational evidence supports divergent outcomes rather than wholesale replacement, though it is not specific to legal AI.
qs: Under the key assumption, discussed next, that remaining non-automatable tasks of accounting clerks and inventory clerks must still be performed by workers in those occupations, we anticipate that routine task-replacing automation will raise expertise demands in the accounting clerk occupation and lower them in the inventory clerk occupation.

As shown in Figure 13 and detailed in Table 5C, all four point estimates are qualitatively consistent with predictions: task expertise gains predict employment reductions, regardless of whether these gains stem from task removal or task addition; task removal predicts employment reductions; and task addition predicts employment gains.

st.t: Labour evidence: Distinct mechanisms resist one AI effect
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s methodological conclusion that the Expertise material is too incomplete to substantiate labour-market findings or legal-staffing implications. Its fragments lack headings, explanatory prose and interpretable claims, so they cannot establish a unified AI effect or resolve current displacement debates.

kp.k: Automation can replace experts while complementing expertise
kp.d: Autor and Thompson propose a cross-domain economic framework rather than a study of legal services. Automation's occupational effects depend on the expertise of removed tasks relative to remaining tasks, not simply the amount of work exposed. The same automated task can remove scarce expertise from one occupation while freeing workers for more expert work in another.
qs: Since the same task may be relatively expert in one occupation and inexpert in another, automation can simultaneously replace experts in some occupations while augmenting expertise in others.

kp.k: Bundled tasks make expertise an occupational entry barrier
kp.d: The model assumes hierarchical expertise: more expert workers can perform less expert tasks, but not vice versa. Each worker must perform all non-automated tasks bundled within an occupation, so its most demanding task determines eligibility. Automation can therefore expand qualified labor supply by eliminating an expertise barrier. The authors do not model why bundling occurs, suggesting communication frictions and proximity requirements as possible explanations.
qs: Workers must perform all non-automated tasks in an occupation, so entry into each occupation is limited to workers capable of performing its most expert task.
We do not model why tasks of different expertise levels are bundled in occupations

kp.k: Expertise changes predict opposing wage and employment movements
kp.d: The framework predicts that falling expertise requirements lower occupational wages while allowing less expert workers to enter; rising requirements increase wages while constraining relative employment. This differs from task-quantity changes, which operate like labor-demand shifts. In the formal model, employment in remaining expert occupations stays constant, declining relative to newly inexpert occupations rather than necessarily falling absolutely.
qs: automation that decreases expertise requirements reduces wages but permits the entry of less expert workers; automation that raises requirements raises wages but reduces the set of qualified workers.
Falling occupational expertise requirements therefore operate like outwards shifts in the labor sup- ply curve: as expertise barriers to an occupation fall, its employment rises and its wage falls.

kp.k: Productivity gains do not guarantee universal worker gains
kp.d: Under the model's assumptions, automation increases output but harms workers whose formerly scarce expertise becomes redundant. Newly inexpert occupations initially expand as entry barriers disappear, then gradually lose employment as subsequent automation makes other occupations more productive. These are theoretical results conditional on assumptions including fixed labor and capital supplies, non-automatable generic tasks, sufficiently productive automation, and an occupational demand elasticity exceeding one.
qs: Automation is always output-increasing in the model but never Pareto-improving.
Entry causes wages in newly inexpert occupations to fall to the level of all other inexpert occupations.
With a fixed capital stock this result is not automatic.

kp.k: Accounting and inventory clerks illustrate divergent occupational outcomes
kp.d: The authors contrast accounting clerks, whose remaining work includes specialized problem-solving, with stock and inventory clerks, whose remaining work includes relatively inexpert physical tasks. Between 1980 and 2018, bookkeepers and accounting and auditing clerks declined from 1.62 million to 1.11 million workers while mean log real wages increased from 2.57 to 2.90 ($13.07 to $18.17). Stock and inventory clerks increased from 0.538 million to 1.48 million workers while mean log real hourly earnings fell from 2.66 to 2.52 ($14.30 to $12.43). The authors present these contrasting historical patterns as consistent with their framework.
qs: Alongside their automatable routine tasks, core accounting tasks include numerous non-automatable problem-solving and decision-making tasks requiring specialized knowledge and training (what we term expertise).

Because automation eliminates primarily expert tasks in the inventory clerk occupation—for instance, flagging when items are below the government support price—our framework predicts that required expertise and hence relative wages in that oc- cupation will decline.

kp.k: Expertise is measured through specialized vocabulary
kp.d: The authors construct a content-agnostic expertise measure grounded in the Efficient Coding Hypothesis, using word frequency and entropy rather than interpreting task descriptions' meaning. They use the Standard Frequency Index for 140,000 English words drawn from 60,000 text samples, adjust it using the Dale-Chall readability list, subtract it from 100, and aggregate word scores to tasks and occupations. They distinguish specialized vocabulary from conceptual complexity and acknowledge that vague descriptions, common-word combinations, and archaic terms can distort measurement.
qs: The Efficient Coding Hypothesis implies that words with high frequency and high entropy are non-specialized, while those with low frequency and low entropy are typically used by experts.
For clarity, we also subtract the SFI from 100 so that it is increasing in expertise.
A shortcoming of the SFI is that it will tend to underestimate expertise in cases where: job tasks are under-specified

kp.k: Semantic matching identifies historical task additions and removals
kp.d: The analysis matches 1977 Dictionary of Occupational Titles tasks with 2018 O*NET tasks using OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, 1,536 dimensions, and a Euclidean-distance caliper of 0.95 derived through manual verification of 600 proposed matches. It links the resulting retained, removed, and added tasks to 303 harmonized Census/ACS occupations and 1980–2018 earnings and employment. Expertise changes exclude wording changes in retained tasks. Task addition is externally compared with new occupational titles from a separate Census source, yielding a coefficient of 4.49 (SE 1.36).
qs: Text embeddings enable us to match tasks on their semantic content rather than particularities of wording.
Removed tasks are those that are present in 1977 but lack a sufficiently close 2018 counterpart.
Added tasks are those that are present in 2018 but lack a sufficiently close 1977 counterpart.

kp.k: Measured expertise predicts wages beyond educational attainment
kp.d: Across 303 occupations, one standard deviation greater measured expertise is associated with wage differences of 16 and 31 log points in 1980 and 2018; the corresponding coefficients are 0.164 (SE 0.014) and 0.305 (SE 0.018), with bivariate R-squared values of 0.32 and 0.49. The relationship remains positive with education and broad occupational controls. The authors identify managers and executives as a measurement exception, attributing their negative gradient to broad, vague task descriptions rather than correcting the scores.
qs: The explanatory power of expertise is high, with bivariate R-squared values of 0.32 in 1980 and 0.49 in 2018, respectively (much of which is retained even after controlling for education).

The inclusion of these covariates reduces the expertise slope, as expected, but in all cases, XPT has robust predictive power for earnings, with a t-ratio never below 5 and a partial R-squared value of 0.09 or higher.

kp.k: Expertise and task quantities independently predict wage changes
kp.d: In longitudinal regressions controlling for broad occupational categories, net expertise change predicts wage growth with coefficient 0.175 (SE 0.047), while net task change has coefficient 0.334 (SE 0.123). Separating removal and addition yields positive expertise-change coefficients of 0.147 (SE 0.051) and 0.255 (SE 0.088). Thus removing inexpert tasks or adding expert tasks predicts wage gains, while the reverse predicts losses. Task addition independently predicts higher wages; the task-removal coefficient is negative but less precisely estimated. The authors cannot confidently separate worker-composition changes from changes in occupational wage premia.
qs: Both expertise change and task change individually and jointly predict occupational wage change, and this remains true whether or not occupation group main effects are included.

Because neither task quantity removal nor task quantity addition has any intrinsic relationship to task expertise change, either task removal or task addition can raise or lower expertise requirements.
we lack sufficient precision to confidently differentiate these mechanisms.

kp.k: Employment evidence distinguishes expertise from task quantity
kp.d: For 1980–2018, the controlled employment regression gives net expertise change a coefficient of −0.510 (SE 0.199) and net task change 1.430 (SE 0.523): higher expertise predicts lower relative employment, whereas additional tasks predict employment growth. Excluding four occupations with extreme employment contraction leaves the main pattern intact. Decomposition results are driven principally by task removal; the task-addition coefficients have the predicted signs but are imprecise. The authors acknowledge that the outliers challenge their assumption that every occupation retains non-automatable generic tasks.
qs: This implies that a 0.1σ rise in occupational task expertise predicts a 6.9 log points (relative) fall in employment over the corresponding decade.
We caveat that most of the identifying variation for these estimates stems from task removal, both through its effects on task expertise and task quantity.
These examples run counter to our model

kp.k: Routine-task automation helps explain divergent wage trajectories
kp.d: Using GPT 4.1 task classifications, the authors estimate that routine tasks constituted 50.37% of raw task counts in 1977 and 32.22% in 2018; 66.06% of removed tasks were routine, while 77.11% of added tasks were abstract. Manual review agreed with the classifier in 89% of 100 cases. Their intended causal test uses hypothetical removal of all initially routine tasks to predict expertise changes. In the 300-occupation baseline, expertise-gain exposure predicts wage gains with coefficient 0.053 (SE 0.009), while task-loss exposure predicts wage declines with coefficient −0.103 (SE 0.041). This supports their explanation that routine automation can either deskill or increase remaining expertise requirements.
qs: We use the systematic elimination of routine tasks between 1977 and 2018 to provide identifying variation for changes in task expertise and task quantities by occupation.
Routine task removal bifurcated occupational expertise demands—and wages along with them.

kp.k: Routine-exposure employment results depend on excluding outliers
kp.d: The routine-exposure employment findings are weaker than the wage findings. In the 300-occupation baseline joint regression, expertise-gain exposure has coefficient −0.016 (SE 0.040) and task-loss exposure −0.002 (SE 0.187), neither statistically significant. After excluding four extreme-contraction occupations, the expertise coefficient becomes −0.163 (SE 0.041) in 296 occupations; task-loss exposure remains insignificant at 0.040 (SE 0.169). This qualification limits the strength of the paper's broader summary claims about employment bifurcation.
qs: But neither point estimate is statistically significant.
Trimming substantially increases the precision of the employment estimates, however.
Our estimates suggest instead that rising expertise requirements more than falling task quantities contribute to falling employment in formerly routine task-intensive occupations.

kp.k: AI relevance is conceptual rather than directly measured
kp.d: The empirical evidence concerns the computer revolution and ends in 2018, not contemporary generative-AI adoption or legal-service outcomes. The authors propose applying the framework to AI and other technological epochs, but explicitly characterize the evidence as illustrative rather than definitive. Their theoretical model is not directly estimable; empirical implementation substitutes average task expertise for the model's maximum expertise requirement, and extends the framework symmetrically to task addition even though new tasks are not formally modeled.
qs: Our conceptual model is illustrative but not directly estimable.

We are implicitly mapping the maximum expertise required in an occupation, which is the relevant object in the model, to the average expertise required in an occupation, which is the relevant object in the data.
Our model does not consider the addition of new occupational tasks
the empirical evidence presented here— based on a relatively coarse set of occupations studied over a relatively short interval—should be viewed as illustrative rather than definitive

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Autor and Thompson argue that automation can simultaneously replace experts and complement expertise, depending on which tasks it removes relative to those that remain.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain labour-market source, not a study of legal services. The authors predict that automating relatively expert tasks lowers occupational expertise barriers, reduces incumbent wages and enables less-expert workers to enter. Automating relatively inexpert supporting tasks instead increases the scarcity value of remaining expertise, raising wages while lowering relative employment. They distinguish these expertise effects from task-quantity effects: gaining tasks predicts higher wages and employment, whereas losing tasks predicts employment contraction. They also argue that adding expert tasks or removing inexpert tasks predicts wage gains, while adding inexpert tasks or removing expert tasks predicts wage declines. In their formal model, employment initially jumps when an occupation loses its remaining expertise requirements, then gradually contracts as automation advances elsewhere. These are theoretical predictions tested against historical computerisation; application to AI is proposed rather than directly demonstrated.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors offer a general-equilibrium model and historical US occupational evidence, rather than measurements of contemporary AI deployment.
pts.d: They combine 1977 Dictionary of Occupational Titles and 2018 O*NET task descriptions with wages and employment for 303 harmonised US occupations in the 1980 Census and 2018 American Community Survey. Their expertise index uses word frequency and entropy; embeddings identify retained, removed and added tasks. GPT-4.1 classifies routine, abstract and manual tasks, with author agreement in 89 of 100 manually reviewed classifications. In regressions controlling for task quantities and broad occupation groups, net expertise change predicts wage change with a coefficient of 0.175 (standard error 0.047) and employment change with a coefficient of −0.510 (0.199). The authors additionally present a causal interpretation of exposure to hypothetical removal of occupations' initial routine tasks. In that analysis, expertise-gain exposure predicts wage gains, but its employment relationship is statistically insignificant in the baseline sample and becomes significantly negative after excluding four occupations with extreme employment declines. Employment estimates associated with task addition are imprecise. The authors explicitly describe the overall evidence as illustrative rather than definitive; these historical results are not direct estimates of AI's effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical timeframe is the computerisation era, approximately 1977–2018; the authors propose applicability to AI without a dated forecast.
pts.d: The June 2025 paper measures task changes over 1977–2018 and wage and employment changes over 1980–2018, generally reporting decadalised changes. Its mechanism depends on hierarchical expertise and occupational task bundling: workers must be capable of performing every remaining non-automated task in their occupation. The model assumes generic tasks remain human-performed, fixed aggregate supplies of labour and capital, sufficiently productive automation, and an elasticity of substitution between occupational outputs greater than one. Employment in still-expert occupations remains constant in the formal model and declines relative to newly inexpert occupations, rather than necessarily falling absolutely. The empirical implementation uses average expertise, whereas the formal entry barrier is the most expert required task. Task addition is treated symmetrically in the empirical analysis but is not explicitly modelled. The authors acknowledge occupations with near-complete displacement as counterexamples to their assumption that generic human tasks remain. Their extension to AI supplies neither a deployment schedule nor a quantitative forecast for particular professions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted winners and losers are differentiated by occupational task bundles and expertise barriers, not simply by exposure to automation.
pts.d: Incumbents whose scarce expertise remains necessary gain from automation of supporting tasks. Incumbents whose expertise becomes redundant face lower occupational wages and competition from newly eligible, less-expert entrants; those entrants can gain access to higher-paying work. Accounting clerks and stock and inventory clerks illustrate the contrast: the authors report accounting-related employment falling from 1.62 million to 1.11 million during 1980–2018 while real hourly earnings rose from $13.07 to $18.17; stock and inventory clerk employment rose from 0.538 million to 1.48 million while earnings fell from $14.30 to $12.43. These are historical occupational comparisons, not predictions of the same outcomes for lawyers. The model also predicts rising returns to a fixed capital stock as automation expands. The source does not make specific claims about law-firm staffing, legal pricing, clients or access to justice.
